answer_text:
The parametrization is

\[
t(r,\phi)=(r\cos\phi,\; r\sin\phi,\; r^2),
\qquad r\ge 0,\quad 0\le \phi\le 2\pi.
\]

We need

\[
\iint_S \frac{1}{(1+4z)^2}\,dS.
\]

First compute the surface element \(dS\).

\[
t_r=(\cos\phi,\sin\phi,2r),
\qquad
t_\phi=(-r\sin\phi,r\cos\phi,0).
\]

Then

\[
t_r\times t_\phi
=
\begin{vmatrix}
\mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k\\
\cos\phi & \sin\phi & 2r\\
-r\sin\phi & r\cos\phi & 0
\end{vmatrix}
=
(-2r^2\cos\phi,\,-2r^2\sin\phi,\,r).
\]

Thus

\[
\|t_r\times t_\phi\|
=
\sqrt{4r^4+r^2}
=
r\sqrt{1+4r^2}.
\]

So

\[
dS=r\sqrt{1+4r^2}\,dr\,d\phi.
\]

On the surface, \(z=r^2\), so

\[
\frac{1}{(1+4z)^2}
=
\frac{1}{(1+4r^2)^2}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\iint_S \frac{1}{(1+4z)^2}\,dS
=
\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty
\frac{1}{(1+4r^2)^2}
\left(r\sqrt{1+4r^2}\right)\,dr\,d\phi.
\]

Simplify the integrand:

\[
\frac{r\sqrt{1+4r^2}}{(1+4r^2)^2}
=
\frac{r}{(1+4r^2)^{3/2}}.
\]

Hence

\[
\iint_S \frac{1}{(1+4z)^2}\,dS
=
\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty
\frac{r}{(1+4r^2)^{3/2}}
\,dr\,d\phi.
\]

Evaluate the \(r\)-integral. Let

\[
u=1+4r^2,
\qquad du=8r\,dr,
\qquad r\,dr=\frac{du}{8}.
\]

When \(r=0\), \(u=1\); as \(r\to\infty\), \(u\to\infty\). Thus

\[
\int_0^\infty \frac{r}{(1+4r^2)^{3/2}}\,dr
=
\frac18\int_1^\infty u^{-3/2}\,du.
\]

Now

\[
\int u^{-3/2}\,du=-2u^{-1/2},
\]

so

\[
\frac18\int_1^\infty u^{-3/2}\,du
=
\frac18\left[-2u^{-1/2}\right]_1^\infty
=
\frac18(2)
=
\frac14.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\iint_S \frac{1}{(1+4z)^2}\,dS
=
\int_0^{2\pi}\frac14\,d\phi
=
\frac14(2\pi)
=
\frac{\pi}{2}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\frac{\pi}{2}}
\]
